title: Hydroxy compounds
overview: Understand the chemistry of phenol alongside alcohols, and further synthetic routes between them. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Form esters from alcohols/phenols and acyl chlorides.
Describe preparation and reactions of phenol.
Explain acidity differences among water, phenol, alcohols and carboxylic acids.
Explain activated ring substitution and 2,4,6 direction by –OH.

definitions.definition: A compound with –OH directly attached to an aromatic ring.
C₆H₅O⁻, the conjugate base of phenol.
Tendency to donate H⁺; stronger acids form more stable conjugate bases.
An aromatic compound containing the –N₂⁺ group, formed cold from a primary aromatic amine.
A coloured compound containing an –N=N– link between carbon groups.
Introduction of an acyl group, often by reaction with an acyl chloride.

sections.title: Alcohol acylation
content: Alcohols react with acyl chlorides at room temperature to form esters and HCl. This is faster and more complete than acid-catalysed esterification. Name the ester by the alcohol-derived alkyl group followed by the acid-derived carboxylate.
bullets: Acyl chlorides fume in moist air because hydrolysis releases HCl.
Keep the carbonyl oxygen in the acyl fragment.

sections.title: Making and reacting phenol
content: Phenylamine reacts with HNO₂ generated from NaNO₂/dilute acid below 10 °C to form a diazonium salt; warming with water gives phenol. Phenol reacts with Na or NaOH to form phenoxide, with dilute HNO₃ at room temperature to give 2-/4-nitrophenol, and with Br₂(aq) to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
bullets: Cold conditions stabilise the diazonium ion.
Bromination gives a white precipitate and decolourises bromine water.

sections.title: Acidity
content: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because negative charge in phenoxide is delocalised into the ring; ethoxide has no comparable stabilisation. Phenol is less acidic than carboxylic acids, whose carboxylate charge is delocalised equally over two electronegative oxygen atoms.
bullets: Phenol reacts with NaOH but not normally Na₂CO₃.

sections.title: Activated ring and azo coupling
content: The –OH group donates electron density into the ring, activating it and directing substitution to 2,4,6 positions, so phenol nitrates/brominates under milder conditions than benzene. In alkaline solution, phenoxide couples with a diazonium ion to form an azo dye.
bullets: Show the –N=N– linkage in an azo product.

examTips: Use conjugate-base structures when comparing acid strength.
Attach conditions to phenol reactions because they distinguish them from benzene reactions.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Saying phenol is a typical alcohol.
Using concentrated nitrating mixture as the only phenol nitration condition.
Claiming phenoxide charge stays only on oxygen.

quickRecall.question: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
quickRecall.answer: Phenoxide is resonance-stabilised by delocalisation into the aromatic ring; ethoxide is not.

quickRecall.question: How is phenol made from phenylamine?
quickRecall.answer: Diazotise below 10 °C with HNO₂, then warm the diazonium salt with water.

quickRecall.question: Why does phenol brominate without AlBr₃?
quickRecall.answer: –OH donates electron density and activates the ring.
